title.text:
Judging a model: metrics,
leakage and imbalance

objects.text: How do we tell a model that works from one that only looks good?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 16 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you built two models that give each loan a probability of default, and you chose a decision threshold on the training loans from the cost of a mistake. Today the question is harder. How do we tell a model that works from one that only looks good?

We stay with the same loans. You will read a confusion matrix, say what precision and recall mean in plain words, and catch a model that cheats.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can read a confusion matrix and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from its four counts. You can read an ROC curve and a precision-recall curve, and choose the metric that fits the cost of each mistake.

And you can find a column that leaks the answer and test a model with stratified cross-validation. In the lab you will do all of this on the same loans as last session.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python lab in Colab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 15 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures and follow the arithmetic. After a ten minute break you open the Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab.

You will compute each measure yourself first, then check it against scikit-learn. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A logistic regression gives a loan p = 0.30. What does that number mean?
2.  Why is 0.50 rarely the right decision threshold?
3.  What does one-hot encoding do?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 15. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A logistic regression gives a loan p = 0.30. What does that number mean?

A good answer is this. The model estimates a 30 percent chance that the loan defaults. A decision threshold turns that probability into a yes or no.

Question two. Why is 0.50 rarely the right decision threshold?

A good answer is this. A missed default and a false alarm cost different amounts. At 0.50 our model flags only 67 of 2,000 loans and misses 200 of the 251 defaults.

Question three. What does one-hot encoding do?

A good answer is this. It turns a text variable such as occupation into one 0 or 1 indicator column per category, so a model can use it.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A table that counts every kind of right and wrong prediction: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
Precision: of the loans flagged, the share that defaulted. Recall: of the loans that defaulted, the share flagged. F1 combines both.
The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall, sensitivity) against the false positive rate at every threshold. AUC, the area under it, is 0.5 for a coin flip and 1.0 for a perfect model.
A feature that contains the answer, or information only known after the outcome. It makes a model look brilliant and fail in real use.
Test the model k times, each time on a different fold, with every fold keeping the same share of defaults. Average the scores. Use it to tune before you test.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN). A table that counts every kind of right and wrong prediction: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

Precision, recall and F1. Precision: of the loans flagged, the share that defaulted. Recall: of the loans that defaulted, the share flagged. F1 combines both.

ROC curve and AUC. The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall, sensitivity) against the false positive rate at every threshold. AUC, the area under it, is 0.5 for a coin flip and 1.0 for a perfect model.

Data leakage (target leakage). A feature that contains the answer, or information only known after the outcome. It makes a model look brilliant and fail in real use.

Stratified k-fold cross-validation. Test the model k times, each time on a different fold, with every fold keeping the same share of defaults. Average the scores. Use it to tune before you test.

title.text:
A baseline model that flags nobody
is right 87.45 percent of the time

objects.text: 1,749 of the 2,000 test loans were repaid. Saying "no default" for every loan is correct for all of them, and it finds none of the 251 defaults.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_bcf2b87b.png
objects.alt: A baseline model that flags nobody is right 87.45 percent of the time

slides.notes:
Start with a trick question. Take the baseline model from Session 14: it says no default for every loan. On our 2,000 test loans, which hold 251 defaults, 1,749 were repaid, so the baseline is right 87.45 percent of the time. It looks like a strong number, and it finds none of the 251 defaults.

The reason is class imbalance: the positive class is rare, so the majority class wins by doing nothing. The share of answers that are right is called accuracy, and today we see why it cannot be the only number we look at. Would you hire a credit officer who approves every loan?

title.text:
The confusion matrix counts every
kind of right and wrong prediction

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_confusion_7.70x4.80_ca34f138.png
objects.alt: The confusion matrix counts every kind of right and wrong prediction

objects.text: Logistic regression at threshold 0.20 on the 2,000 test loans.

runs.text: Rows: what really happened (actual). Columns: what the model said (predicted).
Positive class: default. Negative class: repaid.
Each loan lands in exactly one of the four cells.

slides.notes:
This table is the most useful picture for judging a classifier. It is called a confusion matrix, and it is just a count table. In Excel you would build it with COUNTIFS. The rows are what really happened and the columns are what the model said. We use the scikit-learn layout, with the negative class first.

These are the 2,000 test loans at a threshold of point two. Bottom right, true positives: 108 defaults the model flagged. Top right, false positives: 170 repaid loans flagged by mistake. Bottom left, false negatives: 143 defaults the model missed. Top left, true negatives: 1,579 repaid loans rightly cleared.

The four numbers add up to 2,000. Which cell worries a lender most?

title.text:
Each cell has a name: the second word is the
prediction, the first says whether it was right

rows.text: Flagged, and it really defaulted: a good catch.
Flagged, but the loan was repaid: a false alarm.
Not flagged, but it defaulted: a missed default.
Not flagged, and it was repaid: rightly cleared.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shield_0.50.png

objects.text: In pandas: ((y_pred == 1) & (y_test == 1)).sum() counts the true positives. A type I error is a false positive, a type II error a false negative (Session 12).

slides.notes:
Here are the four names. The second word is what the model predicted: positive means flagged, negative means cleared. The first word says whether the prediction was right: true or false. So a false positive is flagged but wrong, a false alarm, and a false negative is cleared but wrong, a missed default.

At threshold point two we have 108 true positives, 170 false positives, 143 false negatives and 1,579 true negatives. If you studied statistics, a false positive is a type one error and a false negative is a type two error, as in Session 12. Which of the four counts would you report to a credit committee first?

title.text:
Accuracy is the share of right answers,
and it can reward doing nothing

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.31_8ba36e8c.png
objects.alt: Accuracy is the share of right answers, and it can reward doing nothing

rows.text: True positives and true negatives: the right answers
False positives and false negatives: the wrong answers
The baseline has higher accuracy and catches no default

objects.text: Accuracy paradox: with a rare positive class, accuracy can rise while the model gets less useful.

slides.notes:
Accuracy is the number of right answers divided by all answers. Our model at threshold point two has 108 true positives and 1,579 true negatives, out of 2,000 loans, so accuracy is 0.844. Now the baseline that flags nobody: no true positives, but 1,749 true negatives, so its accuracy is 0.875.

The baseline beats our model on accuracy, yet it finds no defaults. That is the accuracy paradox: when the positive class is rare, accuracy rewards doing nothing. So we need measures that look at the positive class on purpose. Is a high accuracy ever enough?

title.text:
The accuracy paradox: the model that
finds nothing has a high accuracy

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_groupbars_11.90x4.25_a41a5bea.png
objects.alt: The accuracy paradox: the model that finds nothing has a high accuracy

objects.text: Recall: the share of the 251 defaults flagged. Accuracy falls as the model finds more.

slides.notes:
Look at the gold bars, recall, the share of the 251 real defaults that the model flags. The baseline has recall zero and an accuracy of 0.87, within 2 points of the model at point five. At a threshold of point five the model has accuracy 0.89 and recall 0.20: it finds only one default in five.

At point two accuracy drops to 0.84 and recall rises to 0.43. At point one recall reaches 0.70 and accuracy is 0.65. The model that is more useful has a lower accuracy. Which bar would you show your manager?

title.text:
Precision and recall each ask a different
question about the positive class

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.51_129a7e41.png
objects.alt: Precision and recall each ask a different question about the positive class

rows.text: Of the loans flagged, the share that really defaulted
Of the loans that defaulted, the share flagged. Also sensitivity or true positive rate
All loans that defaulted (the actual-positive row)

slides.notes:
Precision and recall both start from the true positives, but divide by different things. Precision divides by everything we flagged, true positives plus false positives. It answers: when the model says default, how often is it right?

Here 108 divided by 278 is 0.388, about 39 percent. Recall divides by everything that really defaulted, true positives plus false negatives. It answers: of the real defaults, how many did we catch?

108 divided by 251 is 0.430, about 43 percent. Recall is also called sensitivity or the true positive rate. Which of the two would a lender with little cash worry about first?

title.text: Precision reads down the column of flagged loans

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_confusion_7.70x4.80_c774a372.png
objects.alt: Precision reads down the column of flagged loans

objects.text: Of 278 loans flagged, 108 defaulted: precision 0.39.

runs.text: High precision: few false alarms. A flag can be trusted.
Watch it when each flag costs a person's time, such as a manual review.
Low here: about 61 percent of flags are good borrowers.

slides.notes:
Here is precision as a picture. The gold column holds every loan the model flagged: 108 true positives and 170 false positives, 278 in all. Precision is the gold cell divided by the whole column, 0.39. So when this model says default, it is right about 39 percent of the time, and about 61 percent of the flags are good borrowers.

Precision matters most when each flag costs something, for example when a fraud analyst must review every flagged transaction by hand. What would a precision of ninety percent let you do?

title.text:
Recall reads along the row
of loans that really defaulted

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_confusion_7.70x4.80_12e4a685.png
objects.alt: Recall reads along the row of loans that really defaulted

objects.text: Of 251 defaults, 108 were flagged: recall 0.43.

runs.text: High recall: few missed defaults.
Watch it when a miss is expensive, as in lending, disease screening and fraud.
Here the model misses 143 of the 251 defaults.

slides.notes:
And recall as a picture. The gold row holds every loan that really defaulted: 108 caught and 143 missed, 251 in all. Recall is the gold cell divided by the whole row, 0.43. The model finds about 43 percent of the defaults and misses the other 57 percent.

Recall matters most when a miss is expensive, as with a lender who never recovers a defaulted loan, or a clinic that must not miss a sick patient. Notice that you can always get recall of one hundred percent by flagging every loan. That is why recall alone is not enough.

Why would that be a bad model?

title.text:
F1 combines precision and recall in one
number, and punishes a big gap between them

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.31_6f76ad65.png
objects.alt: F1 combines precision and recall in one number, and punishes a big gap between them

rows.text: Precision 1.00 and recall 0.01: the mean is 0.505, F1 is
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall
One number to compare thresholds or models when both mistakes matter

objects.text: F1 ignores the true negatives. It is 0 when nothing is caught and 1 when every flag is right and every default is found.

slides.notes:
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. At threshold point two, precision is 0.388 and recall 0.430, and F1 is 0.408. Why do we avoid the plain average of the two?

Imagine a model that flags one loan, gets it right, and finds one in a hundred defaults: precision one, recall point zero one. The plain mean says point five, which sounds respectable. F1 says 0.020, which is honest. F1 stays low unless both numbers are decent. It ignores true negatives completely, and it treats precision and recall as equally important, which a lender may not.

Where would you want a weighted version?

title.text:
Every threshold gives different metrics, and F1 is highest
at 0.20 of these five (0.17 if you check every step of 0.01)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_switch_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.39.png

objects.text: Baseline for comparison: accuracy 0.875, recall 0. Logistic regression on 2,000 test loans. Gold: F1.

slides.notes:
Now the same four measures at five thresholds. As the threshold falls, recall rises from 0.20 to 0.70, because we flag more loans. Precision falls from 0.76 to 0.22, because more of the flags are false alarms. Accuracy falls too. F1, the gold column, is highest at 0.20 in this list, with 0.408.

Searching every threshold in steps of point zero one, the best F1 is at 0.17. No threshold wins on every column. The choice depends on which mistake costs more. Which row would you choose for a lender with plenty of cash?

title.text:
Raising the threshold buys
precision and spends recall

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_curve_11.90x4.25_e45da757.png
objects.alt: Raising the threshold buys precision and spends recall

objects.text: Logistic regression on the 2,000 test loans, thresholds 0.02 to 0.60.

slides.notes:
This picture draws the table for every threshold. The red line is recall: it is high when the threshold is low and falls as we raise it. The black line is precision: it climbs as the threshold rises, although it gets jumpy on the right where only a few loans are flagged.

The dashed line is F1, which peaks in the middle, here near 0.17, and the gold dot marks it. No threshold gives high precision and high recall together, because the model cannot separate every defaulter from every good borrower. A better model pushes both lines up. Where do the red and black lines cross?

title.text:
Choose the metric from the cost
of the mistake, not from habit

rows.text: A lender who cannot recover a defaulted loan.
A fraud team that can review only 50 cases a day.
Both matter and the classes are lopsided
Comparing two thresholds in one number.
You need the quality of the ranking, before choosing a threshold
The classes are balanced and the costs are equal

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Which measure should you report?

Ask which mistake costs more. If missing a positive is the expensive mistake, as with an unrecovered loan, watch recall. If false alarms are expensive, as when a fraud team can review only fifty cases a day, watch precision. If both matter and the classes are lopsided, F1 gives one number.

If you want to judge the quality of the ranking before you pick a threshold, use AUC, which we meet next. Accuracy is fine only when the classes are balanced and the mistakes cost the same, which is rare. Which row describes your own work?

title.text:
The ROC curve plots the true positive rate
against the false positive rate at every threshold

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_curve_11.90x4.25_97dbf3f6.png
objects.alt: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold

objects.text: Each dot is one threshold. Lower threshold: more defaults caught, more false alarms.

slides.notes:
The ROC curve, short for receiver operating characteristic, draws every threshold on one picture. Up is the true positive rate, which is recall, also called sensitivity: the share of defaults caught. Across is the false positive rate: the share of repaid loans that were flagged by mistake. Each dot is a threshold.

At point five we sit near the bottom left: false positive rate 0.01, recall 0.20. At point two we reach recall 0.43 for a false positive rate of 0.10. At point one, recall 0.70 and false positive rate 0.35. The dashed diagonal is a coin flip. The further the curve bows towards the top left, the better the model.

Which threshold would you pick on this curve?

title.text:
AUC 0.76: a random defaulter outranks a
random repaid loan 76 percent of the time

objects.text: 251 defaults and 1,749 repaid loans make 438,999 pairs. In 331,793 the defaulter ranks higher. 0.50 is a coin flip. Gini = 2 x AUC - 1 = 0.51.

slides.notes:
AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and it has a friendly meaning. Take one loan that defaulted and one that was repaid, both picked at random. The AUC is the chance that the model gave the defaulter the higher probability. We have 251 defaults and 1,749 repaid test loans, which makes 438,999 pairs.

In 331,793 of them the defaulter ranks higher, and that share is 0.756. A coin flip scores point five and a perfect model scores one. As a rule of thumb, 0.5 to 0.7 is weak, 0.7 to 0.8 is fair, and above 0.9 deserves a leakage check. Credit teams report the Gini coefficient, two times AUC minus one, here 0.51.

How would you describe a fair model to a manager?

title.text:
The precision-recall curve is the clearer
view when the positive class is rare

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_curve_11.90x4.25_f77d051f.png
objects.alt: The precision-recall curve is the clearer view when the positive class is rare

objects.text: Each dot is one threshold. A model with no skill sits on the dashed line.

slides.notes:
The precision recall curve plots precision against recall at every threshold. Here a model with no skill would flag loans at random and have a precision equal to the default rate in the test set, 0.126, the dashed line. Our model sits well above it. At point five, precision is 0.76 but recall only 0.20.

At point one, recall is 0.70 and precision has fallen to 0.22. When the positive class is rare, this curve is more honest than the ROC curve, because the ROC curve counts the huge number of true negatives and can look flattering. Which curve would you show a risk committee?

title.text:
class_weight="balanced" makes each rare
default count more when the model learns

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_weights_11.90x4.25_eab232a2.png
objects.alt: class_weight="balanced" makes each rare default count more when the model learns

objects.text: Weight = rows / (2 x rows in class). Each default counts like 7.0 repaid loans.

slides.notes:
Class imbalance means the model sees far more repaid loans than defaults: 5,247 against 753 in the training set. A model trained on that can drift toward always saying no. The setting class weight equal to balanced gives each row a weight, the number of training rows divided by two times the rows in its class.

A repaid loan gets 0.57, a default gets 3.98. So each default counts like 7.0 repaid loans, and both classes carry the same total weight, about 3,000. Why might that change what the model predicts?

title.text:
class_weight shifts the probabilities upward,
but the ranking and the AUC hardly change

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_switch_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.39.png

objects.text: On the 2,000 test loans. Balanced weights at 0.50 behave like the plain model at a threshold near 0.13.

slides.notes:
Here is what the weights do. With the usual threshold of point five, the plain model flags 67 loans and has recall 0.20. The balanced model flags 569 loans and has recall 0.62, with a lower precision of 0.27. That is very close to what the plain model does at a threshold of about 0.13, which you can see in the last row.

The AUC barely moves, 0.756 against 0.756, because the ranking of loans is nearly the same. So class weight is another way of moving the decision threshold, and it distorts the probabilities, so they no longer mean a true chance. If you need honest probabilities, keep the plain model and move the threshold.

Which would you prefer?

title.text:
Target leakage: collection_calls is
recorded only after the loan has gone bad

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_leak_timeline_11.90x4.25_a5f63fcc.png
objects.alt: Target leakage: collection_calls is recorded only after the loan has gone bad

objects.text: A feature is usable only if it exists at the moment the lender must decide.

slides.notes:
Now a danger that has fooled many professionals. Data leakage means the model sees information it would not have in real use. Here the loans file has a column called collection calls. It counts the phone calls the collections team made to the borrower. Those calls happen only after a borrower stops paying.

On the timeline, the lender must decide at approval, the red dashed line. Application and approval data exists then. The collection calls come after the default. The data dictionary says it plainly: the column is recorded only after a loan goes bad. A model that uses it is told the answer by the answer.

This kind is called target leakage. Which columns in your own files appear only after the outcome?

Here is how you would find a leaked column. Compare the column across the two outcomes. Defaulted loans average 4.55 calls and repaid loans 0.24. Every single defaulted loan has at least one call. The correlation of collection calls with default is 0.87, far above the next strongest variable, the instalment-to-income ratio, at 0.37.

A feature that predicts almost perfectly and is recorded after the event is the signature of target leakage. The honest question is when the feature is recorded. Who in your organisation could tell you when each column is filled in?

title.text:
An AUC of 0.996 should make you suspicious:
the leaky model peeks at the answer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_curve_11.90x4.25_b1b1026b.png
objects.alt: An AUC of 0.996 should make you suspicious: the leaky model peeks at the answer

objects.text: Same loans, same method. At 0.20 the leaky model shows precision 0.88, recall 0.96.

slides.notes:
Add collection calls to the features and fit the same logistic regression. The red curve hugs the top left corner: AUC 0.996. The honest model, in black, has 0.756. At a threshold of point two the leaky model reports precision 0.88 and recall 0.96, against 0.39 and 0.43 for the honest one.

It looks wonderful. But it would fail on the day you use it, because a new applicant has no collection calls yet. The rule of thumb: a result that looks too good to be true usually is. Investigate before you celebrate. What would you ask the analyst who showed you this curve?

title.text:
Leakage has several forms, and
each has a habit that prevents it

rows.text: Target leakage: a feature recorded after the outcome
Ask when each column is recorded. Drop what is not known at decision time.
Train-test contamination: test rows influence training
Filling missing income with the median of all loans, before the split
Split first. Fit imputers and scalers on the training set only. A scikit-learn Pipeline does this.
The same borrower in the training and test sets
Remove duplicates before splitting, or split by borrower.
Using next month's repayment to predict this month
Split by date: train on the past, test on the future.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clock_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Target leakage is the most famous form, but not the only one. Train test contamination happens when information from the test rows reaches the model, for example when you fill missing incomes with the median of all loans before you split. The fix is to split first and fit every imputer and scaler on the training set only, which a scikit-learn pipeline does for you.

Duplicates can sit in both sets, so the model has seen the test borrower already. And in time series, using the future to predict the past is leakage too, so split by date. Note that in Sessions 14 and 15 we computed the median income before splitting, on purpose: a small contamination that we accepted for teaching.

The safe-order slide of Session 14 shows the pipeline version. Which form could affect your data?

title.text:
Stratified 5-fold cross-validation tests the model
five times, each fold with the same default rate

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_folds_11.90x4.25_39b86d4b.png
objects.alt: Stratified 5-fold cross-validation tests the model five times, each fold with the same default rate

objects.text: Five folds of 1,600 loans from all 8,000. Every loan is in the validation fold (gold) once.

slides.notes:
One train test split can be lucky or unlucky. Cross-validation repeats the test. We cut the 8,000 loans into five folds. In each round, one fold is the validation fold, in gold, and the other four train the model, in black. Stratified means each fold keeps the same share of defaults as the whole file: 1,600 loans and 200 or 201 defaults in every fold, so no fold is accidentally easy.

The file is in date order, so without shuffling each fold is a block of months. The five AUC scores are 0.770, 0.782, 0.710, 0.754, 0.769. Their mean is 0.757 and the standard deviation is 0.028. The spread tells you how much one lucky split could mislead. Why report the spread as well as the mean?

title.text:
Cross-validation agrees: the honest model is about
0.76, and the leaky one is too good to be true

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.39.png

objects.text: AUC on each validation fold of the 8,000 loans. Std: sample standard deviation. Cross-validation cannot detect leakage by itself: the leaked column is in every fold.

slides.notes:
Here are all five rounds for the two models. The honest model scores between 0.71 and 0.78, mean 0.757. The leaky model scores above 0.996 in every round, mean 0.996. Notice an important point: cross-validation did not catch the leak. The leaked column is available in every fold, so every fold looks wonderful.

Cross-validation tells you whether a score is stable. It cannot tell you whether the score is honest. Only asking when a column is recorded can do that. Which job does cross-validation do, and which job does the question when is it recorded do?

Tune before you test: choose settings on a validation set
or by cross-validation, then score the test loans once

objects.text: Tuning on the test loans makes the final score optimistic. A validation set is a hold-out part of the training loans; cross-validation repeats that hold-out five times.

slides.notes:
This is the habit that protects every score you report. A model has three jobs, and each job gets its own loans. Fitting the parameters uses the training loans. Tuning the settings, such as the decision threshold or the depth of a tree, called hyperparameters, uses a validation set, which is a part of the training loans held out for comparing choices.

Cross-validation does the same five times, and we used it in Session 15 to find the threshold of 0.10. On the 6,000 training loans the five folds of 1,200 loans give an AUC of 0.748 with a spread of 0.007. Only then do we score the 2,000 test loans, once, and get 0.756.

If you tune on the test loans, the final score is optimistic. Which job is the easiest to get wrong?

runs.text: Line 1: the four counts as a 2 by 2 array. flag is the yes or no at your threshold.
Line 2: precision, recall and F1 for each class in one table.
Line 3: AUC from the probabilities, not from the yes or no flags.

Before the lab, read the recipe. Line one returns the confusion matrix as a two by two array, with the negative class first. Lines four and five create a logistic regression with balanced class weights, and the max iter of one thousand avoids a ConvergenceWarning. In the lab it sits inside the same pipeline as the Session 15 model. Lines six and seven define five stratified folds and score the model on each one by AUC.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: AUC is about 0.6 (0.60 for flags at 0.50) instead of 0.76
You passed yes or no flags, not probabilities.
Pass y_prob, the probability column, to roc_auc_score.
Confusion matrix is the wrong way round
scikit-learn puts the negative class first.
Read it as TN and FP on top, FN and TP below.
Precision gives a zero division warning
Nothing was flagged, so TP + FP is 0.
Lower the threshold, or pass zero_division=0.
Drop it from the honest features.
Fold scores differ a lot from the single split
Report the mean and the standard deviation.

Five messages you may meet. An AUC around point six, point five eight to point six seven depending on the threshold, means you passed yes or no flags instead of probabilities. The confusion matrix has the negative class first, so the true positives are bottom right. A zero division warning on precision means nothing was flagged, so lower the threshold.

A cross-validation AUC of point nine nine means the leaked column is still in your features. And folds that differ from your single split are normal, so report the mean and the spread. If a yellow ConvergenceWarning appears, raise max iter or scale the features. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

compare with the short answers

rows.text: A model has 95 percent accuracy on a file where 5 percent of cases are positive. Is it good?
Not necessarily. Saying negative for every case also gives 95 percent. Check recall and precision for the positive class.
Precision is 0.40 and recall is 0.60. Say each in a sentence about flagged loans.
Of the loans flagged, 40 percent defaulted. Of the loans that defaulted, 60 percent were flagged.
A feature gives an AUC of 0.99. What is the first question to ask?
When is this feature recorded? If it is only known after the outcome, it is leakage and must be dropped.
